extracted.subtask_description: Advice and craft criteria for producing and evaluating genre fiction (especially horror), including idea generation, character development, authenticity of voice/setting, persistence in drafting, and market/length considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must move me emotionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King lists this as his first flaw in a discarded draft: if the material doesn't engage the writer emotionally, it's unlikely to work for readers. Anti-pattern: continuing with a story you don't feel, because emotional distance usually produces flat work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling lead character
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead needs to be interesting and not merely a passive, ready-made victim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King disliked the original Carrie as 'thick and passive.' A protagonist should provoke curiosity or sympathy; a passive character who elicits no feeling from the writer is a sign to rethink characterization or point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial authority/authenticity with subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: You should feel at home with the surroundings and the cast; lacking that authority weakens the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King felt he’d 'landed on Planet Female' and wasn't at home writing an all-girl cast. If you lack lived experience, you must research, recruit knowledgeable readers, or rethink scope. Anti-pattern: writing outside your understanding without doing the work to make it convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural payoff and appropriate length/market fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the story will pay off only if it is a certain length and whether that length fits the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King judged the idea wouldn't pay off unless it was 'pretty long' and thus might not suit men's magazines' word-count limits. Consider whether an idea sustains the required narrative length and whether that length matches intended outlets (and their commercial realities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance through difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't stop a piece just because it's hard emotionally or imaginatively; sometimes you must go on when you don't feel like it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King warns that stopping because a piece is hard is a mistake: 'Sometimes you have to go on when you don’t feel like it.' He also notes you may be producing good work even when it feels like you're 'shoveling shit from a sitting position.' Anti-pattern: abandoning projects at first deep resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine real-life memories and observation for detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use personal memories and observed people/places as raw material to build characters and scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King dug back into memories of real classmates (Sondra, Dodie) to inform Carrie and her classmates. Concrete, specific recollections (appearance, gestures, family context) provide texture and believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine disparate ideas to generate premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring together unrelated ideas or details (e.g., adolescent cruelty + telekinesis) to spark original plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King describes two unrelated ideas merging into the basis for Carrie. Guidance: keep an open mind to odd juxtapositions; cultivate broad reading and experience so disparate elements can collide productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek and value outside feedback/help
rubrics_metrics.description: Show early drafts to trusted readers and accept practical input; collaborators can provide facts, perspective, and encouragement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabby retrieved thrown-away pages, urged continuation, and supplied factual detail (e.g., napkin dispensers). Practical help from informed readers can rescue a project or point out its potential. Anti-pattern: isolating yourself and discarding drafts without a second opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to revise original perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the writer's initial perception of characters may be wrong and be prepared to revise that view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King notes: 'the writer’s original perception of a character or characters may be as erroneous as the reader’s.' This is a reason to revise, reframe POV, or deepen characterization rather than cling to first impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do factual research for credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Check factual details (institutional practices, objects, procedures) to increase realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tabby corrected King about sanitary-napkin dispensers not usually being coin-op. Small factual errors undermine credibility; simple research or asking knowledgeable readers prevents avoidable mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market realities and craft with them in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of where and how you plan to publish (pay rates, word counts, audience expectations) and let that inform decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King weighed the economics of men's magazines, Playboy pay rates, and paperback rights when deciding how to proceed. While art shouldn't be wholly subservient to market, pragmatic awareness helps you choose form and length or whether to pursue a different outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor intimate, sensory writing when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: King's personal stylistic preference: writing is best when it's intimate, 'as sexy as skin on skin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This advocates for close, tactile, sensory prose that evokes immediacy and intimacy. It's presented as a personal rule: if your natural strength is intimacy, lean into it. Anti-pattern: stilted, distant narration when intimacy is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not shy away from distasteful or difficult territory if it's necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploring unpleasant or distasteful subjects may be essential to truthful storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King admits he 'rarely... explored more distasteful territory' but did so to understand Carrie. If a story demands uncomfortable material, handle it honestly rather than avoid it; ensure you have the craft and ethical perspective to handle it responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature permanent discard of drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Before throwing away pages for good, consider re-evaluation or getting another reader—what seems useless may contain the basis of a career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King crumpled pages and threw them away, but Tabby rescued them and urged him to continue; the manuscript became Carrie. Anti-pattern: irrevocably deleting early work without backup or second opinion.
